I'll review the module for logic bugs, panics, overflow, undefined behavior, and concurrency issues.The module corrupts stock counts, panics on ordinary inputs, has three undefined-behavior holes, and can deadlock in `Service`.

### Inventory accounting

`available` does a raw `on_hand - reserved`. Any state where `reserved` exceeds `on_hand` panics in debug builds and wraps in release builds. `low_stock` calls this twice, so it hits the same fault.

`receive` always `insert`s a brand-new `Item`. For an SKU that is already present, the previous `on_hand` and `reserved` are discarded and replaced by the new `qty` with `reserved: 0`. A second receipt of an existing SKU shrinks stock and drops outstanding reservations, so later `ship` calls no longer match the holds.

`release` uses `saturating_sub` and returns `Ok(())` when `qty` is larger than `reserved`. The reservation count collapses to zero, including units reserved for other callers.

`record_loss` does `on_hand -= lost` with no check. `lost > on_hand` panics in debug and wraps in release (stock becomes huge). A smaller loss that still eats into reserved units leaves `reserved > on_hand`, which is the state that breaks `available` and `ship`.

`ship` checks `qty` only against `reserved`, then decrements `reserved` before `on_hand`. When `on_hand < qty`, the `on_hand` subtraction panics or wraps after `reserved` has already changed.

`total_value` multiplies `on_hand as u64 * price_cents` and sums the products in `u64`. Either step overflows: debug panic, release wrap.

### `deltas`

```rust
for i in 0..prices.len() {
    out.push(prices[i + 1] - prices[i]);
}
```

On every non-empty slice the last `i` is `len - 1`, so `prices[i + 1]` panics. For two or more prices, earlier iterations run first and `i64` subtraction can overflow (`i64::MAX - (-1)`, `i64::MIN - 1`): panic in debug, wrap in release. An empty slice returns an empty vec and is fine.

### Undefined behavior

`SlotTable::lookup` calls `get_unchecked` on a slot the comment says comes from a scanner. `slot >= slots.len()` is undefined behavior.

`append_batch` stores `buf.as_ptr().wrapping_add(start)`, then calls `extend_from_slice`, then dereferences that pointer. The `&mut` use invalidates it, and any reallocation frees the buffer. The read is a use-after-free. `head` already holds that SKU.

`decode` builds a `String` with `from_utf8_unchecked` on bytes it describes as a network record. Invalid UTF-8 is undefined behavior. The length check only prevents a short buffer; it does not validate UTF-8.

### Codec

`encode` stores `name.len() as u8`. Lengths above 255 truncate (300 becomes 44, 256 becomes 0). `decode` then treats the front of the name as the whole name and reads the SKU and quantity from the wrong offset, returning `Ok` with corrupted fields. If that truncated prefix splits a multibyte character, the unchecked UTF-8 read in `decode` is undefined behavior on `encode`'s own output.

### `Service` concurrency and holds

Lock order is inverted:

- `place_hold` and `sweep_expired` take `warehouse`, then `holds`.
- `confirm` takes `holds`, then `warehouse` (both the expiry `release` and the `ship` path).

One thread in `place_hold` or `sweep_expired` holding `warehouse` and waiting for `holds`, and another in `confirm` holding `holds` and waiting for `warehouse`, deadlock.

`place_hold` calls `reserve` before `Instant::now() + ttl`. That addition panics when `ttl` does not fit in `Instant` (`Duration::MAX` and other large values). The panic happens after the stock is reserved and before the hold is inserted, so nothing will ever `release` or `sweep` those units. Unwind also poisons the `warehouse` and `holds` mutexes; later `lock().unwrap()` calls panic.

ISSUES:
L47: available() subtracts reserved from on_hand unchecked, so reserved > on_hand panics in debug and wraps in release
L81: receive() overwrites an existing SKU, discarding current on_hand and reserved and keeping only the new qty
L101: release() saturates and returns Ok when qty exceeds reserved, clearing reservations it should reject
L112: ship() decrements on_hand with no on_hand check after reserved is already reduced, panicking or wrapping when on_hand < qty
L120: record_loss() subtracts lost from on_hand with no check, panicking, wrapping, or leaving reserved above on_hand
L127: total_value() overflows u64 on the per-item multiply or the sum (debug panic, release wrap)
L156: deltas() loops 0..len and reads prices[i + 1], panicking on every non-empty slice
L157: deltas() subtracts i64 values with no overflow check (debug panic, release wrap) on earlier pairs
L185: lookup() uses get_unchecked on scanner input, so an out-of-range slot is undefined behavior
L196: append_batch() dereferences a Vec pointer after extend_from_slice has invalidated it (use-after-free, undefined behavior)
L204: encode() truncates name.len() to u8, so names longer than 255 bytes decode as corrupted sku/qty
L218: decode() uses from_utf8_unchecked on network bytes, so invalid UTF-8 is undefined behavior
L253: Instant::now() + ttl panics on overflow after reserve(), leaking that reservation and poisoning the mutexes
L259: confirm() locks holds then warehouse while place_hold() and sweep_expired() lock warehouse then holds, so they deadlock

I am reviewing the Rust inventory service for logic errors, panics, integer overflow, undefined behavior, memory safety issues, and concurrency problems.

`Item::available()` subtracts `reserved` from `on_hand` without checking for underflow. If reserved exceeds on_hand, the unsigned subtraction wraps in release mode or panics in debug mode.

`record_loss` subtracts lost units from `on_hand` without checking bounds or accounting for reserved stock. This can leave `on_hand` below `reserved`, which triggers the underflow panic in `available()`.

`record_loss` can panic or wrap if `lost` exceeds `on_hand`.

`receive()` replaces existing items with a fresh `Item` instead of adding to the current stock. This overwrites `on_hand`, silently drops `reserved`, and replaces the SKU name and price. It violates the documented contract.

`reserve()` cannot overflow `reserved` because the caller checks availability first. If `on_hand` is below `reserved`, the panic in `available()` occurs before the addition.

`release()` clamps excess releases to zero via `saturating_sub`.

`release()` returns `Result` but never yields `Insufficient`. It only fails for unknown SKUs. Releasing more than reserved is silently clamped to zero. This is inconsistent with `reserve` and `ship`, which check bounds and return errors. It can hide inventory accounting bugs.

`ship()` subtracts `qty` from `on_hand` without checking whether the remaining stock would go negative. This can underflow `on_hand` and corrupt inventory state.

`total_value()` computes `on_hand as u64 * price_cents` and sums the products. This can overflow `u64` multiplication or the running sum, causing silent wrap-around in release mode.

`moving_average()` panics via an `assert!` when the window is zero. This is a runtime panic in a public API.

`moving_average()` would compute NaN if the window were zero, because `0.0 / 0.0` is invalid. The `assert!` prevents this by panicking instead.

`moving_average()` can overflow its `u64` running sum if the daily slice is larger than about 2^32 elements, because each element is a `u32`. On 64-bit machines this is practically impossible.

`deltas()` panics on empty input. The loop index `i` reaches `prices.len()`, so the next iteration reads `prices[len]` and the program aborts.

`deltas()` subtracts adjacent `i64` prices without checking for overflow. This can wrap in release mode or panic in debug mode.

`SlotTable::lookup()` uses `get_unchecked(slot)` on untrusted scanner input. This is undefined behavior if the slot index exceeds the table length.

`SlotTable::lookup()` is only undefined behavior on out-of-bounds access. Empty slots return `None` safely.

`append_batch()` computes a raw pointer with `wrapping_add(start)` and then dereferences it unsafely. This is undefined behavior if the vector reallocated between pushing the head and extending the tail.

`encode()` truncates SKU names longer than 255 bytes to `u8` when writing the length prefix. The decoder then reads the wrong number of bytes, corrupting subsequent fields or silently dropping name data.

`decode()` uses `from_utf8_unchecked` on untrusted network bytes. This is undefined behavior if the payload contains invalid UTF-8.

`decode()` should use `str::from_utf8` and return a `Malformed` error instead of calling `from_utf8_unchecked`. The length guard `rest.len() < len + 8` prevents out-of-bounds reads, and the `try_into().unwrap()` calls on four-byte slices are safe because the preceding check already ensures the buffer is large enough. The `len + 8` arithmetic cannot overflow `usize` since `len` is at most 255.

`Service::place_hold()` acquires the warehouse lock before the holds lock and before the next_id lock. This lock ordering could deadlock against other methods that acquire those same locks in a different sequence.

`confirm()` acquires the holds lock before the warehouse lock. `sweep_expired()` acquires the warehouse lock before the holds lock. This ABBA ordering deadlock can occur when one thread holds the warehouse lock while waiting for the holds lock, and another holds the holds lock while waiting for the warehouse lock.

`place_hold` can permanently reserve stock if the `next_id` lock panics after `reserve` succeeds but before the hold record is inserted. The `*n += 1` increment on the global ID counter can also overflow its `u64` type.

`Instant::now() + ttl` panics when the TTL duration is too large to add to `Instant`. This is a real public API panic bug.

The global hold ID starts at zero and increments before use, so the first valid ID is one. If the counter wraps around, duplicate IDs overwrite existing holds in the HashMap; the old hold's reservation leaks because its quantity remains reserved while the new record replaces it.

In `confirm()`, the expired path removes the hold from the map before calling `release`. If `release` fails because the SKU is unknown, the hold is already gone and the error propagates.

The `release` failure path in `confirm()` is unreachable. The warehouse has no delete method, and `receive` only overwrites an item rather than removing it, so every SKU that can be held always exists.

`ship()` returns `Insufficient` when the requested quantity exceeds `reserved`, but it never mutates the item. If `confirm()` removes the hold before calling `ship()`, a failed shipment leaves the hold record gone while the reservation stays in place, leaking stock.

`sweep_expired` ignores errors from `release` inside its `retain` closure. A failed release leaves the hold record removed and the reserved units unreleased.

`snapshot` clones a warehouse item while holding the lock. Calling `available()` on that clone can still trigger the same underflow panic.

`parse_command` is correct and has no serious bugs.

`receive` overwrites an existing item and resets its `reserved` count to zero. This silently invalidates active holds in the Service that still expect stock to be reserved.

`receive` overwrites an existing item and resets its `reserved` count to zero. It also fails to add the incoming quantity to the existing `on_hand`, so old stock disappears. The documentation says units should be added to what is already on hand, but the code replaces the entire record instead of merging.

`record_loss` can underflow `on_hand` and does not check that the lost quantity is covered by `reserved`.

The orphan reservation bug in `confirm` is likely latent. The Service API does not expose `record_loss`, and the Warehouse is wrapped inside a mutex guard that cannot be extracted, so external callers cannot directly manipulate stock or reserved counts. This makes the failure path where `ship` fails after the hold is already removed effectively unreachable through the public interface.

`release` silently clamps over-releases to zero via `saturating_sub`. Callers see success even when the actual reserved count was smaller, so they may believe stock was freed that was never reserved.

`record_loss` can leave `on_hand` below `reserved`, which causes `available()` to panic in its `low_stock` branch. It also never checks that the lost quantity is covered by `on_hand` or available stock.

`ship()` mutates `reserved` before `on_hand`, so a subsequent underflow leaves the reservation reduced while the stock count is unchanged. The log entry is never pushed, leaving the state inconsistent.

`total_value()` iterates over a `HashMap`, but the sum of `u64` values is commutative, so iteration order does not affect correctness.

`moving_average` converts large `u64` sums to `f64`, so values above 2^53 lose exact precision. This is a real numerical logic defect.

`deltas()` subtracts consecutive prices with plain `i64` subtraction, so it panics in debug builds when the price difference exceeds `i64::MAX` and wraps in release.

A SKU name of exactly 256 bytes is encoded with a zero-length prefix. The decoder then reads an empty name and misaligns the remaining payload, corrupting subsequent fields.

`SlotTable::get_unchecked` is undefined behavior when the slot index is out of bounds; it can read arbitrary memory.

`SlotTable::get_unchecked` is documented as skipping bounds checks on scanner input, so callers may assume out-of-bounds indices return `None`. They actually trigger undefined behavior.

`append_batch` computes a raw pointer with `buf.as_ptr().wrapping_add(start)`, then passes it to `extend_from_slice`. If the buffer reallocates during that call, the pointer becomes dangling and dereferencing it is undefined behavior.

`append_batch` is unnecessarily unsafe because `head` is already available as a local variable, so the raw pointer is not needed.
